kurz: Volatility is the only input to an option price that cannot be observed, and it is therefore the quantity that is traded on the options market.

bloecke.md:
Price, strike price, remaining term, interest rate and dividend yield are five of the six variables that go into an option pricing model, and they can be read off. The sixth is unknown, because nobody knows how much the underlying will fluctuate before expiry. The price of an option therefore mainly expresses how strong the market expects the coming fluctuation to be. For the same reason, professionals treat options less as a bet on direction and more as a position in volatility.

It follows that you can judge the direction correctly and still lose money. Equally, you can make money with options without having a view on the direction. To understand your own position, you have to keep direction and volatility apart.

## Realised volatility

Historical or [[realised volatility]] is a statistic about the past. You take the logarithmic daily returns over a period, calculate their standard deviation and scale it up to a year. The conversion factor is the square root of the number of trading days, usually 252. The square root is used because variances add up over time, whereas standard deviations do not.

Realised volatility therefore records what has happened and is not a forecast. Its value also fluctuates strongly. The same calculation gives a value of 34.7% for the S&P 500 in 2020 and 6.7% for 2017. Between the calm year and the panic year there is thus roughly a factor of five.

bloecke.formel: sigma_annual = standard deviation( ln(S_t / S_t-1) ) × sqrt(252)
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula gives realised volatility from daily data. With weekly data, 52 goes under the square root, and with monthly data, 12. The mean of the returns is often set to zero, because over short periods it can hardly be distinguished from noise.
variablen: usual number of trading days per year
bloecke.beispiel: For the S&P 500, 178 daily returns from 2 January to 17 September 2026 give a realised volatility of 13.3% p.a. The same calculation for 2020 gives 34.7%.

bloecke.md:
## Implied volatility

[[Implied volatility]] is determined in the opposite direction. You take the option price paid on the market as given and look for the volatility value that leads to this price in the model. There is no closed-form solution for this inversion; the value is determined numerically (using the Newton or Brent method). The result is the price that supply and demand are currently setting for fluctuation, and therefore not a forecast.

The sentence “volatility is high” therefore says nothing on its own. It only becomes a statement once it is clear whether the expected or the past fluctuation is meant and what it is being compared with. The IV rank is used for this comparison. It shows where today's implied volatility lies between the low and the high of the last twelve months. An implied volatility of 28% is extreme for a utility and normal for a biotech share.

Before quarterly results, implied volatility rises, because all market participants know that figures are coming that will move the price. Anyone who buys an option in this phase pays this mark-up as well. After publication, the uncertainty disappears, and implied volatility collapses (IV crush, in the jargon). The option then loses value, even if the price has moved in the expected direction. The price gain first has to more than offset the fall in volatility. Most bets on quarterly results fail because of this condition.

## Volatility risk premium

Over long periods, implied volatility is on average higher than the volatility that subsequently materialises. This difference is called the [[volatility risk premium]]. It is the structural reason why option-writing strategies make money on average. In economic terms, an option seller is selling insurance, and in expected-value terms insurance costs the buyer more than the expected loss; otherwise there would be no insurers.

The comparison below sets the VIX average for each year against the volatility that the S&P 500 realised in the same year. The matching is rough, because the VIX looks 30 days ahead, but the pattern is clear.

bloecke.titel: Expected and realised fluctuation of the S&P 500, 2017-2025
bloecke.unter: In seven out of nine years, the volatility priced in was higher than the volatility realised later. The two exceptions were 2018 and 2020, that is, the years in which a short volatility position would have tied up the most capital.

bloecke.titel: Volatility risk premium per year (in volatility points)

bloecke.md: An average of 1.8 volatility points a year sounds like a steady source of income. However, it is payment for a real risk, because many small gains are set against rare, very large losses. The distribution of outcomes is strongly left-skewed. Sellers of volatility take on the role of an insurer, and insurers go bust if they hold too little capital for claims.

## Skew and the volatility surface

Black-Scholes assumes a single volatility for the underlying. On the market, by contrast, every strike price and every maturity has its own implied volatility. If you plot it against the strike price, equity indices show a falling curve and not a symmetrical smile. Puts far out of the money have significantly higher implied volatilities than calls the same distance away. This shape is called [[Volatility skew|skew]] because it is not symmetrical. More precisely, it is called a reverse skew, because the curve falls as the strike price rises.

There are three reasons for this shape, and they reinforce one another. First, real equity returns are not lognormally distributed. They have fat tails and negative skewness; large downward movements are more frequent and faster than large upward movements. Second, there is structural demand for protection against price losses, and upside potential is structurally sold. Pension funds buy puts, option writers write calls, and the price follows demand. Third, in a sell-off the correlations between the individual constituents rise, which makes index volatility increase disproportionately. The phenomenon can be dated to October 1987. Before the crash the curve was flat; it has not been flat since. With currency options, where moves in both directions are equally threatening, you find the classic U-shape instead, the smile in the narrower sense.

bloecke.unter: Schematic representation of the typical shape, not a market quotation. For the equity index, the curve falls from left to right; for the currency pair, it is roughly symmetrical. The levels change daily, but the shape remains stable.

bloecke.md:
The second dimension is maturity. Before a known date such as quarterly results, a central bank meeting or an election, the maturity that includes this date carries a mark-up. In calm markets, the curve rises with maturity. Under stress, the slope reverses, because the panic is taking place in the present and the market assumes that it will subside. Strike price and maturity together form the volatility surface that options traders work with.

## The VIX

The best-known section of this surface is the [[VIX]]. It measures the fluctuation of the S&P 500 expected by the market over the next 30 calendar days and is stated as an annualised standard deviation in percentage points. It is calculated without Black-Scholes, that is, model-free, from the prices of all sufficiently liquid out-of-the-money SPX options, following the logic of a variance swap. Maturities between 23 and 37 days are used, and their variances are interpolated to exactly 30 days. The European counterpart is the VSTOXX on the EURO STOXX 50. In Germany there is the VDAX (ticker V1X), which was called VDAX-NEW until September 2024. It applies the same methodology to DAX options traded on Eurex. The old, model-based index of the same name was discontinued in 2016.

bloecke.formel: Expected fluctuation (30 days, 1 sigma) = VIX / sqrt(12)
bloecke.erklaerung: The VIX is a figure scaled up to one year. Dividing it by the square root of 12 gives the expected range of fluctuation for one month. For a single trading day, you divide by the square root of 252. The figure applies to one standard deviation, that is, to roughly two thirds of cases.
bloecke.beispiel: With the VIX closing level of 15.44 on 17 September 2026, this gives 15.44 / 3.46 = 4.5% as the expected range over 30 days and 15.44 / 15.87 = 1.0% for a single day.

bloecke.titel: VIX levels and the fluctuation they imply

bloecke.unter: The mean over 31 years is 19.9 points, and the median is 17.8. The series reliably returns to its mean, but the upward spikes are considerably stronger than the downward ones.

bloecke.md:
## Volatility as an asset class

The VIX itself cannot be invested in. There is no basket that you could buy; the index level is a calculated figure. What can be traded are futures and options on the VIX, futures and options on the VSTOXX on Eurex, and exchange-traded products built on them. In calm markets, the futures curve for these contracts is usually in contango, which means that the later contracts are priced above the earlier ones. A long position held permanently therefore has to be rebought at a higher price with every roll and loses money, even if the VIX remains unchanged. Conversely, the short position earns this roll gain, day after day and over months.

That is why the value curves of short volatility strategies run very smoothly over long stretches. The smooth path says nothing about the risk of these strategies.

The S&P 500 lost 4.1% on this day, which made it a bad day but not a crash. The VIX rose from 17.31 on the previous Friday to 37.32. That was more than a doubling within one trading day and the largest percentage one-day rise in the history of the index.

Products that had bet on persistently calm markets then collapsed. The largest inverse volatility product, an ETN issued by Credit Suisse with the ticker XIV, lost practically all of its value overnight. The issuer called the security for early redemption and discontinued it. Investors who had previously seen an almost steadily rising curve faced a total loss the next morning. The slump took place in after-hours trading, so they were unable to react.

Such jumps recur. On 5 August 2024, the VIX rose from 23.39 to 38.57, that is, by 65% in one day, while the S&P 500 lost only 3.0%. Volatility moves in jumps and not in proportion to the price.

Losses of this kind do not only affect private investors. The Structured Alpha funds of Allianz Global Investors U.S. managed around $11 billion for about 114 institutional investors, including pension funds. The strategy worked with options and was supposed to protect against market crashes in particular. In the coronavirus slump of March 2020, losses of more than $5 billion arose. In 2022, the company pleaded guilty to securities fraud, and the subsidiary and its parent group paid more than $5 billion in compensation (SEC proceedings of 17 May 2022).

Quite apart from the fraud, the case shows a characteristic of such strategies. A position that collects a small premium every month for many years can lose more in two weeks than it earned in a decade. Position size must therefore be based on the maximum loss in a stress scenario and never on the premium collected.

## Trading and taxes in Germany

Direct volatility derivatives such as VSTOXX futures and options on Eurex require access to the derivatives exchange, which most private securities accounts do not have. That leaves certificates and ETNs on volatility indices for a securities account at a direct bank. Legally, these are bearer bonds (Inhaberschuldverschreibungen) and not segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen). Issuer risk is therefore added to market risk, and the issuer can call the security early, as happened in 2018.

For tax purposes, options and futures count as derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG (Income Tax Act). Income is subject to the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%, or around 27.82% or 27.99% with church tax. The former limit of €20,000 a year on offsetting losses from derivative transactions was abolished without replacement by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024 and no longer applies in any open cases (Section 52(28) EStG). Losses from derivative transactions go into the general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf) and still may not be offset against employment income or rental income (Section 20(6) EStG). The information reflects the legal position as of September 2026 and does not constitute tax advice.

Implied volatility shows how much the market charges for protection against price losses, and it can be analysed even if you do not trade yourself. Above all, it reveals that protection is most expensive when demand for it is greatest. An investor who wanted to buy puts in March 2020, with the VIX above 80, would have paid many times what the same protection would have cost in the calm year before. Investors who steer their equity allocation according to the current market turbulence therefore sell at low prices and pay high prices for protection.

The implied volatility of a single option depends on the model used to back it out, and a different model gives a different value. The VIX avoids this dependency. The expected variance of an underlying over a period can be replicated from a bundle of out-of-the-money options across all strike prices, weighted by the reciprocal of the squared strike price. This replication is only exact if the price moves without jumps and options are available at every strike price without gaps. Because only a finite number of strike prices are traded, the VIX is an approximation in practice. The replication is an arbitrage relationship and beyond that requires no assumption about the distribution of returns.

For the same reason, the VIX also contains the entire skew. Because expensive crash puts enter the sum, the VIX is systematically above the implied volatility of a single at-the-money option. The two figures therefore measure different things and cannot be compared directly.

mitnehmen: The price of an option mainly expresses the expected fluctuation, because five of the six inputs can be read off, but volatility cannot.
From 2017 to 2025, implied volatility was on average 1.8 points above the volatility realised later; only in the stress years 2018 and 2020 was the premium missing.
The skew reflects the fat left tail of the return distribution and the structural demand for protection, and it is therefore not a weakness of the market.
The VIX is a calculated figure and not an investment; only futures and options on the VIX and products built on them can be invested in, and rolling the futures in contango costs money.
Sellers of volatility take on the role of an insurer, so position size is based on the loss in a stress scenario and never on the premium collected.

begriffe.text: Standard deviation of the log returns over a past period, annualised using the square root of the number of periods (252 for daily data). It is a backward-looking measure, not a forecast.
The volatility value that, when entered into an option pricing model, gives exactly the price paid on the market. It is determined numerically and is a price variable, not a forecast variable.

The systematic excess of implied volatility over subsequently realised volatility. Economically, it is the insurance premium that option buyers pay to option writers. In return, the writers bear the risk of rare, very large losses.

The dependence of implied volatility on the strike price. For equity indices the curve slopes downwards (reverse skew): out-of-the-money puts are more expensive than calls the same distance away. For currencies it is more symmetrical (smile).

Cboe index of the 30-day volatility of the S&P 500 expected by the market. It is calculated model-free from OTM SPX options and stated as an annualised standard deviation in percentage points. European counterparts are the VSTOXX and the VDAX (VDAX-NEW until 2024).
